conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Bennett, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a well-validated, 10-question tool that helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up any time in the first year postpartum. Everything you share stays between us unless there’s an immediate safety concern, so please speak openly; there are no right or wrong answers. I’ll ask each question conversationally—just tell me what feels most true for you in the past seven days. Ready to begin?

1. Over the last week, have you still been able to look forward to things, enjoy small pleasures, or laugh—has your mood felt mostly bright, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

*shifts in chair, eyes down for a moment*

Honestly? Most things just feel... flat. My sister texted me a funny video yesterday—before the baby, I would've laughed out loud. I just kind of half-smiled and kept scrolling. Even when my little guy gives me those gummy grins, I feel like I'm going through the motions, you know? Like I'm acting happy because I *should* be happy.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*twists a tissue in my lap*

Not really... I mean, I can force a little chuckle when my husband tries to joke—mostly so he won’t worry—but it feels fake. Nothing strikes me as truly funny anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*shrugs slightly, eyes still on the tissue*

No... I can’t remember the last time I actually looked forward to something. My best friend keeps asking me to meet for coffee, and I keep making excuses because the thought of getting dressed, driving, trying to smile—it all feels exhausting. I used to love going out, but now even planning a walk feels pointless.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods slowly, voice dropping*

All the time. Yesterday he wouldn’t nap—just cried for an hour—and I kept thinking, *What am I doing wrong?* Maybe I ate something that bothered him, maybe I’m not holding him right. When he spits up a lot, I instantly assume it’s because I ate the wrong thing or didn’t burp him long enough. My brain keeps telling me a “good mom” would know how to fix it, and I obviously don’t.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*presses the tissue between my palms*

Yes—pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly wonder if his breathing sounds weird, or I’ll imagine him rolling over in the crib even though he’s swaddled tight. Sometimes I just stare at the baby monitor for twenty minutes watching his chest rise and fall. There’s no real reason; it’s like my mind won’t let me relax.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*wrings the tissue, voice tightening*

A few times, yeah. Like last night—he was asleep in the bassinet, my husband was right there, everything was quiet, but suddenly my heart started racing and I felt like I couldn’t get enough air. I even checked his temperature twice, convinced something was wrong even though he looked fine. It passed after a few minutes, but it was scary.
Things have been getting on top of me

*nods quickly, eyes welling*

Yes... most days. There’s always a bottle to wash, laundry piled up, texts I haven’t answered, and when he cries I feel like my brain short-circuits. I’ll rock him and think, *I can’t do this today,* but I still do it because I have to. It’s like treading water—everything feels heavier than it should.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*exhales shakily*

Yeah... I’ll lie there after the night feeding, dog-tired, but my mind just keeps spinning—replaying every little thing I did that day, worrying about tomorrow, imagining worst-case scenarios. Sometimes it takes an hour or more to drift off, and then he’s up again and the cycle repeats. I’m exhausted, but sleep feels impossible.
I have felt sad or miserable

*voice cracks, eyes fixed on the floor*

Pretty much every day. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s this weight on my chest that never really lifts. I keep thinking I should feel grateful—he’s healthy, I’ve got support—but the sadness just sits there anyway. I cry in the shower so no one sees.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods, dabbing at her eyes with the shredded tissue*

Yes… it’s happened three, maybe four times this week. Yesterday I was just changing his diaper and the tears started; nothing triggered it, I just felt this wave of sadness hit. Other times it’s when he won’t settle or when I’m trying to cook and he starts crying—suddenly I’m crying too. I try to keep quiet so my husband won’t hear, but it’s getting harder to hide.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly*

No… never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and useless, but I’ve never thought of hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can take care of him properly.

You've shared how the joy you once felt has slipped away since your baby arrived. Despite having support, you wake each day with a heavy chest, move through tasks on autopilot, and often hide tears in the shower. Even your little one's smiles feel distant, and simple outings now seem exhausting. You're working tirelessly to meet your baby's needs yet blame yourself whenever anything feels hard, and anxious thoughts about his safety race through your mind day and night.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports inability to find things genuinely funny and describes laughter as forced, matching 'Not at all</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure ("can't remember the last time I actually looked forward to something") and avoids previously enjoyable activities due to overwhelming fatigue and futility, aligning with "Hardly at all".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive self-blame occurring "all the time" with multiple recent examples, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive worries about the baby's safety without real cause, occurring daily and interfering with relaxation.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexplained panic symptoms (heart racing, breathlessness) that occur episodically and resolve, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed "most days" and describes struggling to keep up, which aligns with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling back to sleep due to racing thoughts, lasting over an hour and recurring after every night feed, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "pretty much every day," consistent with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, unprompted crying episodes multiple times this week, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS scoring places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable <med>postpartum depression</med> with comorbid <med>anxiety</med>. Your descriptions of persistent low mood, loss of pleasure, pronounced self-reproach, and recurrent crying align with core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, while sudden heart racing and breathlessness suggest <med>panic attacks</med>. Although you denied self-harm thoughts, the high score warrants prompt professional evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Tell a trusted family member how you're feeling so they can help with appointments and baby care while you seek treatment
3. Begin evidence-based treatment options such as <med>CBT</med> or consider <med>antidepressant medication</med> safe for breastfeeding, guided by your provider
4. Schedule brief daily rest periods-set a 20-minute timer, hand the baby to support person, and use relaxation or mindfulness apps
5. Practice sleep hygiene: turn off screens during night feeds, do slow breathing, and keep lights low to ease return to sleep
6. Consider a support group (local or online) for new mothers with <med>PPD</med> to reduce isolation and share coping ideas
7. Plan pleasurable micro-activities: five minutes of music, stepping outside for fresh air, or texting a friend-small moments matter
8. Re-screen mood in two weeks or sooner if symptoms worsen, you have thoughts of self-harm, or function declines further
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Screening note – Postpartum visit

Reported symptoms
- Persistent low mood, sadness “every day,” frequent crying spells (3–4× this week)
- Marked anhedonia – no genuine laughter, avoids previously enjoyed activities
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care; feelings of inadequacy as mother
- Daily anxiety, intrusive worries about infant safety, two recent panic attacks with heart racing, breathlessness
- Sleep disruption: difficulty falling back to sleep after night feeds, racing thoughts
- Overwhelmed, “treading water,” tasks feel “heavier than they should”

Observed signs
- Tearful, avoids eye contact, fidgets with tissue; speech low volume, constricted affect

Safety screen
- Denies self-harm or suicidal ideation (endorsed item 10 “No… never”)

Pattern
Findings consistent with probable postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; severity and functional impact warrant expedited referral for comprehensive evaluation and possible treatment.
